content: Zinc is a metallic chemical element represented by the symbol Zn and has an atomic number of 30. Historically, it has also been referred to as spelter in certain contexts, such as in sculpture or historical references. Zinc is a moderately reactive metal with a blue-gray appearance. When exposed to moist air, it tarnishes, and when burned in air, it produces a bright bluish-green flame, releasing zinc oxide as a byproduct. Zinc reacts with acids, alkalis, and non-metals. If the zinc is not completely pure, it reacts with dilute acids to release hydrogen gas. The most common oxidation state of zinc is +2. Between temperatures of 100°C and 210°C (212°F to 410°F), zinc becomes malleable and can be shaped easily. However, above 210°C (410°F), it becomes brittle and can be pulverized. Zinc is nonmagnetic. Zinc plays a critical biological role as an essential element required for the survival of all life forms. It is estimated that approximately 3,000 proteins in the human body contain zinc prosthetic groups, including structures known as zinc fingers. Additionally, over a dozen types of human cells secrete zinc ions, which are now recognized as neurotransmitters. Zinc-secreting cells are found in the salivary glands, prostate, immune system, and intestines. Zinc also activates certain enzymes, such as carbonic anhydrase, which is essential for carbon dioxide transport in vertebrate blood. In plants, zinc is necessary for leaf formation, the synthesis of the growth hormone indole acetic acid (auxin), and anaerobic respiration (alcoholic fermentation). Zinc is naturally present in various food sources. Oysters are particularly rich in zinc, while smaller amounts are found in animal proteins, beans, nuts, almonds, whole grains, pumpkin seeds, and sunflower seeds. Turkey necks and beef cuts like chuck or shank also contain significant amounts of zinc. However, phytates, which are present in whole grain breads, cereals, legumes, and similar products, can inhibit zinc absorption. Clinical studies suggest that zinc, when combined with antioxidants, may slow the progression of age-related macular degeneration. Additionally, adequate dietary zinc intake has been shown to reduce the risk of influenza. Soil conservation studies have examined the uptake of zinc by plants from various soil types. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for zinc in the United States is 11 mg per day for males and 8 mg per day for females, with higher requirements during pregnancy and lactation. Zinc deficiency can result from insufficient dietary intake or poor absorption. Symptoms of zinc deficiency include hair loss, skin lesions, diarrhea, and wasting of body tissues. Zinc is also associated with sensory functions such as eyesight, taste, smell, and memory, and a deficiency can impair these functions. A congenital condition known as acrodermatitis enteropathica is caused by zinc deficiency. Zinc deficiency during pregnancy and early childhood is particularly concerning, as it can impair brain development. Zinc deficiency is also linked to acne and can manifest as leukonychia, or white spots on the fingernails. Zinc deficiency has been implicated as a potential cause of anorexia nervosa (AN). A lack of zinc reduces appetite, which can lead to anorexia nervosa. Appetite disorders, in turn, exacerbate malnutrition, including zinc deficiency. Since 1979, zinc supplementation has been proposed as a treatment for anorexia nervosa. At least 15 clinical trials have demonstrated that zinc supplementation improves weight gain in individuals with anorexia nervosa. A 1994 randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial found that administering 14 mg of zinc per day doubled the rate of body mass increase in patients with anorexia nervosa. Deficiencies in other nutrients, such as tyrosine, tryptophan (precursors to neurotransmitters norepinephrine and serotonin), and vitamin B1 (thiamine), may also contribute to the cycle of malnutrition. While zinc is essential for health, excessive zinc intake can be harmful. Overabsorption of zinc can interfere with the absorption of other essential minerals, such as copper and iron. Free zinc ions in solution are highly toxic to plants, invertebrates, and vertebrate fish. For example, micromolar concentrations of free zinc ions can be lethal to aquatic organisms like daphnia. Ingestion of post-1982 American pennies, which are composed of 97.5% zinc, can damage the stomach lining due to the high solubility of zinc ions in stomach acid. Zinc toxicity is particularly dangerous in dogs, where it can cause severe hemolytic anemia, and in pet parrots, where it is often fatal. Even relatively low levels of zinc intake, such as 100–300 mg per day, can induce copper deficiency. The USDA RDA for zinc is 15 mg per day, but even levels closer to the RDA may interfere with copper and iron metabolism or negatively affect cholesterol levels. Zinc plays a role in the immune system and has antimicrobial properties. Zinc salts are effective against pathogens when applied directly. Zinc has been shown to reduce the severity of gastroenteritis, potentially through its antimicrobial effects in the gastrointestinal tract or through its absorption and subsequent release by immune cells, such as granulocytes. Clinical trials have demonstrated that zinc gluconate and zinc gluconate glycine, commonly used in lozenges, can shorten the duration of common cold symptoms. Zinc oxide is one of the most widely used zinc compounds, serving as a base for white pigments in paint and as an ingredient in opaque sunscreens. It is also used in the rubber industry. Other zinc compounds have industrial applications, such as zinc chloride (used in deodorants), zinc pyrithione (found in anti-dandruff shampoos), zinc sulfide (used in luminescent paints), and organozinc compounds like zinc methyl or zinc diethyl (used in organic chemistry laboratories). Approximately one-quarter of all zinc production is used in the form of zinc compounds. Although metallic zinc is not considered toxic, free zinc ions in solution are highly toxic. Inhalation of freshly formed zinc oxide fumes, such as those produced during the welding of galvanized materials, can cause a condition known as zinc shakes or zinc chills, which is a form of metal fume fever. Excessive zinc intake can also lead to deficiencies in other essential dietary minerals.
